name: Rockridge Cafe
why: Fifty-plus years on College Avenue and a loyal crowd, but the format is a familiar breakfast diner and we found little story beyond the date.
story: A College Avenue breakfast spot that has been cooking from scratch since 1973 and serves breakfast until it closes at 2. The menu runs from migas and pumpkin waffles to challah French toast and ricotta pancakes.
order: The migas, or ricotta pancakes if you're sweet-leaning.
hours: Daily 8 am to 2 pm (Visit Oakland listing)
flags: Story is thin: no owners or family history in a reliable source. 'Family run' appears only on listing sites.
Celebrity-visit claims seen in search summaries were left out (unsourced).

name: 900 Grayson
why: A warehouse-district diner that regulars own in spirit, with a chicken-and-waffles plate that has a name and a kick. Story is solid but not deep: same two brothers for 20 years.
story: A West Berkeley diner where staff tend to know your order. Brothers Chris and Anthony Saulnier have run it since it opened about 20 years ago, and even after a 2010 turn on Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives, they say most customers are neighbors. Plain dining room, sunny patio.
order: The Demon Lover: chicken and waffles, with a spicy kick to the chicken. Or the Grayson burger.
flags: Anthony Saulnier's first name comes from search summaries; 7x7 names only Chris and 'the Saulnier brothers'. Confirm.
Hours not confirmed (7x7 Aug 2026 implies open).
The burger is on an Acme bun per 7x7; left out of the story.

name: Juan's Place
why: A long-running, big-table Mexican room on a West Berkeley corner, cheap enough for a crowd. Story and signature are moderate: the best source is old and the founding details are thin.
story: A corner restaurant in West Berkeley's warehouse blocks, the place locals have long sent big, budget-minded groups. In 2001 the East Bay Express noted it kept winning the paper's Best Mexican readers' poll. Combination plates, enchiladas and burritos, nothing precious.
order: Enchiladas, with the mole if it's on.
flags: Founding year (1972) and the Mejia family name appear only on auto-generated listing sites; not used. Find a real source.
Newest independent coverage found is a 2015 Nosh mention. Confirm still open and current hours.
Mole enchiladas named only on menu aggregators; 'order' is soft.

name: Otaez
why: A family story with real weight: a Fruitvale market kitchen that grew into an Alameda restaurant built on a burned-out landmark's site. The food is classic family Mexican rather than a single famous dish.
story: Named for a town in Durango, Otaez began as a small Fruitvale market kitchen that Jesus and Socorro Campos bought in 1986, he a cook, she a waitress. In 2006 they opened this Alameda restaurant on the site of the old Mexicali Rose branch, which burned during their remodel. Jesus died in 2011; the family still runs both.
order: Chiles rellenos or pozole from Socorro's recipes.
flags: The 1986 purchase and Durango name origin come from an Oakland Latino Chamber page seen in search (now 404). Confirm with the family or another source.
Jesus Campos was killed in 2011 (Patch). The story mentions his death without detail; Dan to decide whether to include it at all.
Two locations (Oakland and Alameda); fine under the chain rule. Confirm both still run by the family.

name: La Selva Taqueria
why: A room you won't forget (jungle murals, disco balls, weekend karaoke) and chicken grilled over charcoal next door. Story is thin: we know it's still with its original owners, little more.
story: You smell it before you see it: whole chickens split and grilled over charcoal in the garage next to the restaurant. Inside it's black walls, disco balls, murals, a black panther statue and a full Lion King scene, with karaoke on weekend nights and a salsa bar served out of a huge molcajete.
order: The pollo al carbón, with the charred-tomatillo salsa verde, which is hotter than it looks.
practical: Karaoke Friday to Sunday from 8 pm
flags: Karaoke schedule from an April 2025 article; confirm.
'Original owners' appears only in a listing summary; no owner names or founding year.
Hours not confirmed.

name: The Original Kadok's
why: A Little Manila standby with a backstory that runs back to a siopao business in the Philippines. The room is casual and the press is thin, which holds atmosphere and story in check.
story: The family business started in the 1980s selling siopao door to door in Bayanan, Muntinlupa, then from a kiosk that added mami noodle soup. In Daly City since the mid-1990s, it's a silog house now: tocino, longganisa, tapa, sisig and crisp smoked bangus, with pancit Malabon by the family tray.
order: Tocino silog for breakfast; add the smoked bangus if you're sharing.
flags: History comes from the restaurant's own site as shown in search results; the site refused our fetch. Confirm details.
Sources disagree on 1994 vs 1995 for the Daly City start; story says mid-1990s.
Owners named as Rick and Pam on one site; not used without a fuller source.

name: Ramen Parlor
why: A ramen shop from the man who built San Mateo's ramen row, in a brick room that looks like an old American diner. The best source is from 2012, so signature and story carry real uncertainty.
story: Kazunori Kobayashi started Santa Ramen in the late 1990s and then Ramen Dojo, which drew lines for its spicy garlic broth. Here, in a cozy brick room that feels like a former coffee shop, the broths lean toward seafood and come with a garlic-lobster oil.
order: The spicy kani miso ramen with soft-shell crab.
hours: Tue-Sun 11 am to 2 pm and 5 to 8 pm, to 8:30 pm Fri-Sat; closed Monday (listing, confirm)
flags: Main source is a 2012 blog post. Confirm the menu (kani miso, lobster oil) and that Kobayashi still owns it.
Hours from a listing aggregator.

name: Shuei-Do Manju Shop
why: The Bay Area's oldest traditional Japanese confectioner, passed between two families on a handshake. A small sweet shop, so the room is modest, but the story and craft are rare.
story: Hatsuyo and John Ozawa founded this Japantown manju shop in 1953. With no children to take it over, John recruited his fishing buddy's daughter and her husband, Judy and Tom Kumamaru, who bought it in 1988 without seeing the kitchen or a recipe. The Ozawas stayed five months to teach them, and everything is still made by hand.
order: A box of mixed manju; the kinako, dusted in soybean powder over white-bean filling, is the one to try.
flags: The 1994 imperial-visit order appears in search summaries and the shop's own history page; not opened, not used.
Hours not confirmed (Edible Silicon Valley piece updated Apr 2026).

name: Donut Basket
why: A family donut shop that locals use like a diner, with cronuts and Vietnamese coffee. The format is common and we found almost no story, so most marks stay low.
story: A family-run donut counter in a North Bayshore strip mall since 2004. Regulars treat it like a diner, coming early for breakfast sandwiches, cronuts, Thai tea and Vietnamese coffee alongside the usual glazed and old-fashioneds.
order: A cronut and a Vietnamese iced coffee.
flags: Weak fit: only the shop's own site and list pages. No press coverage found. Consider dropping.
Cronuts, Thai tea and Vietnamese coffee come from listing summaries, not the shop's site.
Opening time not confirmed.

name: Progressive Grounds
why: A neighborhood living room with a shaded back patio, which is the whole point. There's no signature item and little story, so it scores as a place to sit rather than a place to eat.
story: A Cortland Avenue corner cafe built for staying a while: tables inside, a large shaded patio out back, and enough on the menu to last a whole morning, from wraps and salads to beer and wine. It once had a Mission sibling, which closed around 2016.
order: Coffee and a wrap, taken out to the back patio.
flags: Mission location closure (around 2016) and owner first name 'Marco' come from LocalWiki via search; owner left out.
Infatuation review is from June 2022. Confirm hours and that the patio is still open.
Weak on food: no standout dish anywhere.

name: Panchita's #2
why: The Infatuation puts its pupusas at the top of the city, and the revuelta earns a near-top signature mark. Story is solid: an owner who built a second shop a block from the first and grilled on the sidewalk to get through 2008.
story: A counter-service pupuseria at 16th and Valencia since 1989, a block from the original Panchita's. More than a dozen fillings, all cheesy enough to crisp at the edges, and hundreds made by hand every day. During the 2008 recession the owner put a grill out on the sidewalk to pull in passersby.
order: A revuelta, with extra curtido on top. Two-pupusa deals are the cheap move.
flags: Changed fame to open-secret: the Infatuation lists it among SF's classic restaurants and iconic dishes.
Owner's name and the 2008 grill detail come from the 2021 SFGate piece via search; confirm.
Prices ($4.75 each, 2 for $9.50) from Jan 2025 review; left out of 'order'.

name: Estrellita's Snacks
why: Three generations from a Mission street cart to the Tenderloin's first pupuseria, with real reporting behind it. The food is good rather than famous, which keeps signature in the 70s.
story: Twenty years ago Maria del Carmen Flores pushed a cart of yucca and plantain chips around the Mission. Her daughter Estrella Gonzalez and grandson Angel now run this Ellis Street room, the Tenderloin's first pupuseria. Photos of Maria and her cart hang on the wall next to bright Salvadoran folk paintings.
order: Pupusas and fried yucca. Pan con pollo if you're hungry.
hours: Weekdays 10 am to 8 pm (Mission Local, June 2025; weekends not stated)
flags: Changed fame to open-secret: covered by Mission Local, the Chronicle and CBS.
Mission Local says the owners were worried about their next lease (June 2025). Confirm still open.
Weekend hours unknown.

name: L & G Vietnamese Sandwich
why: A family story few places can match, and bánh mì some neighbors rate above the famous shop across the street. The room is one standing table in the window, so atmosphere stays modest.
story: Ki Giang and Minh Lam met in Cambodia, survived Khmer Rouge work camps, and arrived in San Francisco as refugees. They raised three sons in the Tenderloin and named this little shop for their surnames. It has one standing table in the window, low prices and generous sandwiches, diagonally across from Saigon Sandwich.
order: A roast pork bánh mì, and skip the line across the street.
flags: Address corrected from discovery (401 Larkin St was wrong): it's 602 Eddy St, now matched to OSM node/9735505750.
Hours not found. Mission Local photo essay (Aug 2025) shows it operating.
'Roast pork' is a soft order pick: sources list veggie, chicken, pork, meatball and fish cake but name no favorite.

name: New Lun Ting Cafe
why: A living bachelor's cafe with a counter of regulars and a Hong Kong-meets-British menu you pick by formula. Signature is strong but the food is homestyle, not a destination dish.
story: Chinatown calls it the pork chop house. It opened in 1970 as a bachelor's cafe for single men; when Frances Mah took over from her father in 1989 she pulled out most of the U-shaped bar and added booths for families, but kept a stretch of counter. The bachelors still sit there every day.
order: Pork chop over rice with the brown sauce, a 1970s burnt orange. Ask about the free jello.
hours: Daily 10:30 am to 9:30 pm (Spotlight Chinatown, confirm)
flags: Some sources claim roots back to 1909; Spotlight Chinatown says established 1970. Story uses 1970.
Spotlight profile is undated (likely 2020-21); confirm hours and cash-only.

name: New Woey Loy Goey
why: A basement room with a chop suey sign, a bachelor's counter and Toisan home cooking in claypots: memorable on every count. Story stops short of the top because the early history is unknown.
story: Down a short flight of stairs off Jackson Street, under an old sign still advertising chop suey. Kow Lee took over around 1996, added 'New' to the old name, and swapped the Chinese-American menu for Toisan home cooking served in cast-iron and heavy claypots he sources himself.
order: Steamed pork hash with Chinese sausage, or the lamb claypot. Call a day ahead for the sticky-rice-stuffed chicken.
practical: Glutinous rice chicken needs a day's notice
hours: Daily 11 am to 9:30 pm (Spotlight Chinatown, confirm)
flags: 'Established 1996' in the source likely marks Lee's takeover; the restaurant itself is older. No founding year found.
Spotlight profile undated; confirm BYOB and hours.

name: Eats
why: Fifty years on one corner and passed between owners who wanted to keep it going, but today it's a pleasant brunch cafe more than a one-of-a-kind room.
story: A corner breakfast spot at Clement and Second Avenue since 1975. When it went up for sale in 2009, a regular from up the street, the owner of Burma Superstar, bought it to keep it alive; in 2023 it passed to a new local owner. Expect skillets, breakfast chili and weekend brunch.
order: The spicy tomato skillet with sunny-side eggs, kale and potatoes.
practical: Breakfast and lunch; brunch on weekends
flags: Menu items are from Jan 2023, before the new owner reopened; confirm current menu.
Hours not confirmed.
Joyce Lee's 2009 purchase is from the 2019 Richmond Review via search; not opened.

name: Amphawa Thai Noodle House
why: A chef-owned Thai room with some dishes you don't see on most Richmond menus. Sources are mostly old, so story and signature stay in the middle.
story: Named for the floating market outside Bangkok where vendors cook from their boats. Chef-owner Kob Varaphol ran a Thai restaurant in London before opening here on Geary in 2011. Beyond the usual curries, the house favorites include crying tiger beef, fried pompano with three-flavor sauce, and a pork blood soup for the curious.
order: One of the noodle soups, plus the crying tiger beef to share.
flags: Main source is from 2011. Confirm Varaphol still owns it and the 'Amphawa favorites' are still on the menu (online ordering is live).
Decor and costumed staff details appear only in search summaries; left out.
